quote: So human level intelligence, yes, in principle, but will actual humans-- that might be a sideshow.
claim_summary: Asked whether human-level intelligence is still a good goal for AI, says it is possible in principle but that human-like intelligence may be a sideshow among the many kinds of robot intelligence to come.
definition_note: human level intelligence; he doubts it is the right target
notes: Oral-history interview for the AAAI/MIT CSAIL AI history video project; transcript file (captions) read at the source. Date: at the start of the recording he says "it's 2006", so year precision. Ambiguous field: endorsement. "yes, in principle" affirms that human-level intelligence can be built but does not say it will be, and none of the codebook acceptance words are used, so coded unexpressed rather than accepts. Same interview: he expects robots throughout everyday life within 50 years (not about human-level AI).

quote: Eventually, we will create truly artificial intelligences, with cognition and consciousness recognizably similar to our own. I have no idea how, exactly, this creation will come about. I also don't know when it will happen, although I strongly suspect it won't happen before 2030, the year that some singularitarians predict.
claim_summary: Says humans will eventually create artificial intelligences with cognition and consciousness like ours, does not know when, and strongly suspects not before 2030; argues the singularity will be a gradual period, not a sudden event.
timeline_text: Eventually ... I also don't know when ... I strongly suspect it won't happen before 2030
definition_note: truly artificial intelligences with cognition and consciousness recognizably similar to our own; he calls them AGIs
notes: basis: "Eventually, we will create truly artificial intelligences"; not_by: 2030; Own essay in the IEEE Spectrum singularity special report (June 2008); read at the source; date from the page's published time. source_type blog is the nearest value for a signed magazine essay. Endorsement: the unit says it will come eventually and not before 2030, so accepts with the hedge in timeline_text (codebook: rejecting a near date while accepting eventual arrival). Same essay: "The singularity will be a period, not an event" and "machines will become gradually more intelligent, generation by generation" (the same capability, not split).

quote: In order for there to be a successful volitional AI, especially one that could be successfully malevolent, it would need a direct understanding of the world ... It is going to take a lot of deep thought and hard work from thousands of scientists and engineers. And, most likely, centuries.
claim_summary: Argues that volitional, intentional AI, of the kind that could be malevolent, needs understanding, dexterity and a deep model of humans, and will most likely take centuries; worrying about malevolent AI now is a mistake.
definition_note: volitional or intentional artificially intelligent beings; elsewhere in the essay, human level or super human level intelligence
notes: basis: "It is going to take a lot of deep thought and hard work"; Own essay, first published on the Rethink Robotics blog and reposted on Robohub under his byline; read at Robohub; date from the Robohub byline (11 November 2014). timeline_year left blank: "centuries" gives no number (codebook ruling 11 by analogy with decades). Same essay: "it is a mistake to be worrying about us developing malevolent AI anytime in the next few hundred years" and "Moore's Law applied to this very real technical advance will not by itself bring about human level or super human level intelligence" (a route claim). Target judgment: volitional AI read as broad competence.

quote: The fears of runaway AI systems either conquering humans or making them irrelevant are not even remotely well grounded. Misled by suitcase words, people are making category errors in fungibility of capabilities. These category errors are comparable to seeing more efficient internal combustion engines appearing and jumping to the conclusion that warp drives are just around the corner.
claim_summary: Says fears of runaway AI conquering humans are not remotely well grounded, comparing them to concluding from better car engines that warp drives are near.
timeline_text: not even remotely well grounded ... warp drives are just around the corner
definition_note: runaway AI systems that conquer humans or make them irrelevant
notes: Own answer to the Edge 2015 annual question "What do you think about machines that think?", titled "Mistaking Performance For Competence Misleads Estimates Of AI's 21st Century Promise And Danger"; read at the source. Date: the page gives only the question year 2015, so year precision. elicitation survey because it answers a question put to many contributors; source_type blog is the nearest value for a short signed essay. Ambiguous fields: endorsement and frame. The warp-drive analogy says runaway AI is nowhere near, but the words do not say whether it will ever exist, so endorsement is unexpressed; timeline is present only through the analogy.

quote: "We are going to have more robots, we are going to have more artificial intelligence, but I think people are misinterpreting the progress that is being made," he said. "I don't think we have to worry about that in our lifetime or our children's lifetimes."
claim_summary: Asked about a Terminator-style AI takeover, says it is science fiction, people misread current progress, and it is not something to worry about in our or our children's lifetimes.
timeline_text: I don't think we have to worry about that in our lifetime or our children's lifetimes
definition_note: a Terminator-like Skynet that becomes self-aware (the reporter's framing)
notes: ABC News (Australia) profile with direct quotes from an ABC radio interview; read at the source; date from the page. "that" refers to the reporter's framing of a Skynet takeover, so the target depends on the article text around the quote. Ambiguous field: endorsement. Saying there is no need to worry within two lifetimes implies it will not happen in that time, but the words are about worry, not arrival (codebook: worry is not endorsement), so coded unexpressed with the timing kept in timeline_text. Same piece: "A person can generalise, but we don't have that kind of generalisation in any of these AI learning systems."

quote: Not in our lifetimes, not even in Ray Kurzweil’s lifetime, and despite his fervent wishes, just like the rest of us, he will die within just a few decades. It will be well over 100 years before we see this level in our machines. Maybe many hundred years.
claim_summary: Asked when computers will be as capable as the brain (he revises it to as intelligent and conscious as humans), says not in our lifetimes, well over 100 years, maybe many hundred years; dog-level in maybe 50 to 100 years.
timeline_text: well over 100 years ... Maybe many hundred years
definition_note: computers/robots recognizably as intelligent and as conscious as humans (his revised question)
notes: basis: "It will be well over 100 years before we see this level in our machines"; computed: 2017 + 100; lower_bound; IEEE Spectrum June 2017 special issue "Can We Copy the Brain?", written answers to the magazine's questions; read at the source; date from the page (31 May 2017). Firm minimum ("well over 100 years") with a hedged upper end ("Maybe many hundred years"), coded as an open-ended minimum (A15 ruling 5). Same answer set: "As intelligent and as conscious as dogs? Maybe in 50 to 100 years" and no qualms about human-level AI because the world will have changed too much to predict.

quote: There will be neither benevolent AI nor malevolent AI in the next few decades where AI systems have any internal understanding of those terms. This is a research dream, and I do not criticize people thinking about it as research. I do criticize them thinking that this research is going to turn into reality any time soon
claim_summary: Says there will be no AI with any internal understanding of benevolence or malevolence in the next few decades; such AI is a research dream that will not become reality soon.
timeline_text: neither benevolent AI nor malevolent AI in the next few decades
definition_note: AI systems with internal understanding of ethical terms (intentional AI)
notes: basis: "There will be neither benevolent AI nor malevolent AI in the next few decades"; Own blog, part of the Future of Robotics and Artificial Intelligence series; read at the source; date from the post date in the blog's own feed (2017-08-28). Rejects for the horizon given (next few decades) only; nothing said here about later. Governance is present because the passage criticises talk of regulating such AI. Target judgment: AI with internal understanding read as broad competence.

quote: My own opinion is that of course this is possible in principle. ... However perhaps we humans are just not smart enough to figure out how to do this ... Even if it is possible I  personally think we are far, far further away from understanding how to build AGI than many other pundits might say.
claim_summary: Says AGI is possible in principle, but perhaps humans are not smart enough to build it, and in any case we are far further from knowing how than many pundits say.
timeline_text: far, far further away from understanding how to build AGI than many other pundits might say
definition_note: AGI: autonomous agents that operate much like beings in the world, a thinking entity distinct from current machine learning
notes: basis: "perhaps we humans are just not smart enough to figure out how to do this"; Own blog; read at the source; date from the post date in the blog's feed. The quote keeps the double space after "I" as on the page. MIT Technology Review published an edited version on 2017-10-06 (panel prominence piece); same essay, not recorded twice. Endorsement: possible in principle but perhaps beyond us, so uncertain. Same essay: "We have no idea whether it can even exist" (on AGI as a threat) and, on brain uploading, "hold off on dying for another couple of centuries".

quote: There is not going to be a general intelligence that can suddenly do all sorts of things that humans (or chimpanzees) can do. It is going to be point solutions for a long, long time to come. Building human level intelligence and human level physical capability is really, really hard.
claim_summary: Says no general intelligence will suddenly appear; progress will be point solutions for a long time, human-level intelligence is very hard and we are under 1% of the way there; predicts no robot with a six-year-old's understanding of humans before 2050.
timeline_text: point solutions for a long, long time to come
definition_note: a general intelligence that can do all sorts of things humans can do
notes: basis: "There is not going to be a general intelligence that can suddenly do all sorts of things"; Own blog, the dated-predictions post scored every January since; read at the source; date from the post. Ambiguous field: endorsement. "not going to be ... suddenly" rejects sudden arrival and the next sentence pushes it out "a long, long time", without saying it never comes; coded rejects for the near term. Same post: "In reality we are less than 1% of the way there" (capability_now) and the table item "A robot that has any real idea about its own existence, or the existence of humans in the way that a six year old understands humans" marked NIML (not before 2050). That table is repeated unchanged in every scorecard 2019 to 2026 and is not recorded again.

quote: So, journalists, don’t you dare, don’t you dare, come back to me in ten years and say where is that Artificial General Intelligence that we were promised? It isn’t coming any time soon.
claim_summary: Tells journalists not to come back in ten years asking where AGI is: it is not coming any time soon, and the small groups calling themselves AGI are not making engineering progress.
timeline_text: It isn’t coming any time soon
definition_note: Artificial General Intelligence in the sense the press means; he says it was the goal of AI from the start
notes: basis: "It isn’t coming any time soon"; Own blog, Future of Robotics and AI series; read at the source; date from the post. Rejects near arrival only. The ten years is the journalists' return date, so no not_by year is set (kept conservative). Same post: the AGI groups "in all probability ... will not succeed in decades".

quote: I suspect that human level AI falls into this class. But that it is much more complex than detecting gravity waves, controlled fusion, or even chemistry, and that it will take hundreds of years.
claim_summary: Suspects human-level AI is a problem that will be solved but is harder than gravity waves, fusion or chemistry and will take hundreds of years.
timeline_text: it will take hundreds of years
definition_note: human level AI
notes: basis: "it will take hundreds of years"; Own blog, part I of "Steps Toward Super Intelligence"; read at the source; date from the post. "this class" refers to the preceding passage on hard problems that take a long time but get solved. "I suspect" governs the clause, but no hedge word (may, might, could) is on the date, so accepts. timeline_year blank: no number of centuries. Same post: "it is just really hard, and will take a hundred years, or more, of concerted effort to get there".

quote: Surely it is already solved and Super Intelligence is right around the corner. Again, don’t hold your breath–fifty years is a long time for a human to go without oxygen.
claim_summary: On a demo of a robot assembling furniture: superintelligence is not around the corner; do not hold your breath, as it is at least fifty years away.
timeline_text: don’t hold your breath–fifty years is a long time
definition_note: Super Intelligence: AI beyond human level
notes: basis: "don’t hold your breath"; not_by: 2068; computed: 2018 + 50; Own blog, part III of "Steps Toward Super Intelligence"; read at the source; date from the post. The first sentence is the imagined reader's objection, the second is his answer. Ambiguous fields: endorsement and timeline. The joke implies no superintelligence within fifty years; it says nothing about later, so rejects for that horizon, not acceptance with a minimum.

quote: It is the sort of thing that any Super Intelligence bent on self improvement through code level introspection is going to need in order to understand the code that has been cobbled together by humans to produce it. Without understanding its own code it will not be able to improve itself by rewriting its own code.
claim_summary: Says an AI that improves itself by rewriting its own code would first need to understand messy human-written code, which current AI cannot do.
definition_note: self improvement through code level introspection; rewriting its own code
notes: basis: "Without understanding its own code it will not be able to improve itself"; Own blog, part III of "Steps Toward Super Intelligence"; read at the source; date from the post. Same post as brooks-2018-04a, split by capability (A15 ruling 13). Ambiguous field: endorsement. The words state a condition for self-modification (understanding its own code) and the post argues that condition is far off, but he does not say whether it will be met; coded conditional.

quote: And then, for really the first time in sixty years we will actually be part ways towards machines with human level intelligence and competence. In reality it will just be a small part of the way, and even less of the way to towards Super Intelligence.
claim_summary: Says that even after progress on the research goals he lists, we will only be a small part of the way to human-level intelligence and less to superintelligence.
definition_note: machines with human level intelligence and competence; Super Intelligence beyond that
notes: Own blog, part IV of "Steps Toward Super Intelligence"; read at the source; date from the post. Says current and near-future systems are far from human level, nothing about whether it will come, so unexpressed (ruling 9).

quote: And the claim is that the median estimates from people in the field is that we'll get artificial general intelligence in 2040 and an artificial superintelligence in 2060. And once we get artificial superintelligence, everything's going to go crazy. I think both those numbers are very optimistic.
claim_summary: In his Oxford Strachey Lecture, cites survey medians of AGI by 2040 and superintelligence by 2060 and says both dates are very optimistic.
timeline_text: I think both those numbers are very optimistic
definition_note: artificial general intelligence (as in the survey he cites)
notes: basis: "I think both those numbers are very optimistic"; not_by: 2040; Strachey Lecture "Steps Towards Super Intelligence", University of Oxford; transcript file (machine-made captions, quote as captioned) read at the source; date from the event page cs.ox.ac.uk/seminars/2088 (21 November 2018) and the file name. The event abstract says "why it all could be centuries away" (same occasion, not recorded separately). Same talk: "Are we capable of building human level intelligence? ... maybe we're not."

quote: I may have skewed that average a little as I was an outlier amongst the 18 people at the year 2200. In retrospect I wish I had said 2300 and that is the year I have been using in my recent talks.
claim_summary: Says his answer in Martin Ford's survey of 18 experts (average 2099) was 2200 for AGI, and that he now uses 2300; argues self-driving cars are a lower bound on AGI, so AGI has been delayed.
timeline_text: I wish I had said 2300 and that is the year I have been using in my recent talks
definition_note: AGI, Artificial General Intelligence, with human level capabilities; self driving is a lower bound on it
notes: basis: "that is the year I have been using in my recent talks"; Own blog; read at the source; date from the post. Firm first-person date with no hedge word, so accepts (A15 ruling 1). The survey in Martin Ford's book "Architects of Intelligence" (2018) asked for the year with a 50 percent chance of AGI; his 2200 answer there is known only from this account (the book was not read).

quote: That human level intelligence up there on the Moon is going to be out of reach for a long, long time. We just do not know for how long, but we surely know that we are not going to fly there on winged aircraft.
claim_summary: Using a flight-to-the-Moon analogy, says human-level intelligence will be out of reach for a long, long time, we do not know how long, and current AI methods will not get there.
timeline_text: out of reach for a long, long time. We just do not know for how long
definition_note: human level intelligence
notes: basis: "going to be out of reach for a long, long time"; Own blog; read at the source; date from the post. Coded like "decades away" (ruling 11): arrival far off, with "We just do not know for how long" kept in timeline_text. The route claim in the same post ("No matter how much we improve on our basic architecture of our current AI over the next 100 years, we are just not going to get there") is kept here, not coded (A15 ruling 4). Same post: in expert surveys he predicts "ten or twenty times longer than the second most pessimistic person".

quote: But people who believe we are on the verge of fully general AI see the words it generates, which are rehashes of what it has seen, and believe that it is intelligence. A ouija board.
claim_summary: Says GPT-3 rehashes words it has seen with no model of the world; people who think we are on the verge of fully general AI mistake its output for intelligence.
definition_note: fully general AI
notes: Own blog, annual Predictions Scorecard; read at the source; date from the post. Denies that GPT-3 is or is close to general AI; says nothing about the future, so unexpressed (ruling 9).

quote: This inference of AI arriving momentarily is a clear example of how people mistake performance for competence.
claim_summary: Says the conclusion that GPT-3 and ChatGPT herald the coming of AGI is people mistaking performance for competence; the term AGI is a marketing relabelling of AI's original goal.
definition_note: "AGI" is just "AI" as it was known for its first 50+ years
notes: Own blog; read at the source; date from the post. "AI arriving momentarily" refers to the preceding sentence, that people "jumped to the conclusion that GPT-3 was heralded the coming of “Artificial General Intelligence”", so the target is AGI. Disputes that current systems are close; nothing on the future, so unexpressed.

quote: My impression now is that you do not think the emergence of GPT-4 and other large language models means that an AGI will be possible within a decade or so. Rodney Brooks: You’re exactly right.
claim_summary: Agrees with the interviewer that GPT-4 and other large language models do not mean AGI will be possible within a decade or so; says language models will be useful, better than IBM Watson, but not AGI.
timeline_text: not ... possible within a decade or so
definition_note: artificial general intelligence
notes: basis: "You’re exactly right"; not_by: 2033; computed: 2023 + 10; IEEE Spectrum interview ("Just Calm Down About GPT-4 Already") by Glenn Zorpette, recorded at the Vision, Innovation, and Challenges Summit; read at the source. Date: published 2023-05-17, the interview was at the "recent" summit, so month precision. The proposition is the interviewer's words, which he endorses; the basis is his reply. Same interview: "I think it’s going to be better than that. But not AGI." Scripps News (2023-05-22) reported this interview; the original was used.

quote: I concluded my talk encouraging people to do good things with LLMs but to not believe the conceit that their existence means we are on the verge of Artificial General Intelligence.
claim_summary: Reports ending his MIT Generative AI Week keynote (2023-11-28) by urging people to use language models well but not to believe their existence means AGI is near.
definition_note: Artificial General Intelligence
notes: Own blog, annual Predictions Scorecard; read at the source; date from the post (the talk itself was on 2023-11-28, as the post says; the post is the statement recorded). Hipertextual (2024-01) reported this passage in Spanish. Disputes that AGI is near; no claim about later, so unexpressed.

quote: That quote is from the drone story linked to above, but it could well as been about the hype that we are moving towards AGI (Artificial General Intelligence).
claim_summary: Applies a news line calling the drone sightings a communal fever dream to the hype that we are moving towards AGI; says we are not on the verge of replacing workers, doctors, coders or scientists.
definition_note: AGI (Artificial General Intelligence)
notes: Own blog, annual Predictions Scorecard; read at the source; date from the post. "That quote" is a news line he quotes just before: "perhaps the whole craze has been a sort of communal fever dream". Ambiguous field: present_capability. Calling the move towards AGI hype disputes that we are close, but the words are indirect. Same post, sarcastically: "a year or so ago when ChatGPT was just a baby AGI".

quote: It is the apparent human-ness of these two technologies that both lure people in, and then that promise human level performance everywhere, even when that level has not yet been demonstrated. People think that surely it is just a matter of time.
claim_summary: Says language models and humanoid robots seem human and so promise human-level performance everywhere, though that level has not been demonstrated; people wrongly assume it is just a matter of time.
definition_note: human level performance everywhere
notes: Own blog; read at the source; date from the post. Says human-level performance has not been demonstrated; "just a matter of time" is what other people think, not his own claim, so endorsement unexpressed.

quote: For all his skepticism about robots, Brooks is downright cynical about “superintelligent” AI systems that can out-think humans. Many AI experts believe they’re just a few years away, but Brooks predicts it’ll take three centuries to create them.
claim_summary: Reported as predicting that superintelligent AI systems that out-think humans will take three centuries to create; says in his own words that he spends his later life assuaging fears of things that do not exist.
timeline_text: it’ll take three centuries to create them
definition_note: “superintelligent” AI systems that can out-think humans (reporter's words)
notes: secondhand; basis: "Brooks predicts it’ll take three centuries"; computed: 2026 + 300; Boston Globe profile (business section) based on the reporter's own interview; read at the source; date from the page. The three-centuries figure is the reporter's paraphrase, not a direct quote, so the row is secondhand with low confidence; elicitation interview because the reporter did the interview. His direct words in the same piece: "I did not expect my latter life would be spent assuaging people’s fears of things that don’t exist" (hence present_capability disputed) and "It’s not general intelligence, but it’s useful".
